# The provenance file on Hestía

*Provenance record 210 · Hestía · one temple, fully accounted for.*

## Provenance

**1. The attestation.** **Ἑστία** — "Hearth, fireplace". On record: Hesiod, Theogony 453–458, Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite 7–44, Homeric Hymn 24 to Hestia, Pindar, Nemean 11.1–8.

**2. The preserved evidence.** **i → í** (Acute on short iota) — absent from the ASCII form *hestia*, present in the restoration, verifiable against the sources above.

**3. The narrative record.** **Virginity and Precedence** — Apollo and Poseidon both sought to marry Hestia, and the Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite explains why they failed: Aphrodite's power runs over all gods and men — 'but of the three maidens the mind of Aphrodite cannot win nor ensnare' — Athena, Artemis, and Hestia, who sits 'in the center of the house' and receives the richest portion (Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite 7–44).  Hestia swore a great oath before Zeus to remain a virgin, and Zeus accepted the oath and gave her instead what no marriage could: precedence. **Firstborn and Last Free** — Hesiod makes Hestia the eldest child of Kronos and Rhea — 'their firstborn, and after her wise Zeus' (Theogony 453–458) — which means she was the first to be swallowed by her father and the last to be disgorged when Zeus forced him to surrender his children.  Ancient commentators drew the conclusion her worship already implied: because she went in first and came out last, she receives the first and last portion of every sacrifice, and every libation runs to her before any other god.

**4. The physical record.** Every Greek city maintained a prytaneion housing the public hearth, and their remains anchor the archaeological record: the circular Tholos by the Athenian Agora sheltered the prytaneis' common fire, and monumental prytaneia are excavated at Olympia, Delos, Priene, and Ai-Khanoum in Bactria. At Magnesia on the Maeander, inscriptions mention a round temple of Hestia at the agora's center — civic architecture imitating her flame's geometry. The Roman temple of Vesta in the Forum, rebuilt many times on its archaic round plan, still stands beside the House of the Vestals, and its sisters at Tivoli and elsewhere repeat the form. Public oaths from Samos, Cos, and Thera open with Hestia's name, and her figure appears modestly on votive reliefs — a veiled woman at a small flame — exactly as unassuming as her cult.

**5. The current holding.** The temple at [/hestia/](/hestia/), classified Tier 2. The restoration keeps one feature the ASCII form drops. One is enough to matter, and the label says so plainly: Tier-2.

**6. The documented resonances.** **Food & Hospitality**, **Home, Hearth & Real Estate**, **Wine, Brewing & Hospitality** — seats argued and weighted in the [pattern atlas](/patterns/), read through the myths in this temple's [Resonance File](/hestia/blog/resonance/).

**7. The primary sources.** [Theogony](/texts/theogony/), [Homeric Hymns](/texts/homeric-hymns/), [Works and Days](/texts/works-and-days/) — the library this file answers to, open at the [Sacred Texts collection](/texts/).

**8. The continuing record.** Hestia's legacy is the sanctity of home.  The English word 'hearth' still carries emotional weight far beyond its practical function, and the concepts of hospitality, asylum, and household gods all descend from her cult: to harm a guest seated by the hearth was to profane her.
